subject: Business Models
title: Subsidize One Side
description: A fast breakdown of Subsidize One Side for builders.

hook.text: Uber gave riders $20 credit and drivers guaranteed hourly pay. It literally bought both sides.

buildup.text: Most platforms subsidize the harder side to attract. Once that side joins, the other follows.

discovery.text: Adobe gave away the PDF reader free while charging for the creator. Free readers drove paid creators.

twist.text: Subsidies burn cash fast. Uber lost $31 billion before turning profitable in 2023.

climax.text: Subsidies are temporary bridges. If value doesn't appear by the time subsidies end, the platform dies.

punchline.text: Pay one side, attract the other, then stop paying. If you can.

quiz.question: How much did Uber lose before reaching profitability?

details.summary: Platform businesses often subsidize one side of their market by offering free or below-cost access to attract a critical mass of participants whose presence makes the other side willing to pay premium prices. The paying side funds the entire ecosystem.
details.whyItMatters: Subsidy strategy is one of the most important decisions in platform design. Getting it wrong can burn through capital without reaching critical mass, while getting it right can create an unstoppable growth flywheel.
takeaways: Subsidized users generate value that the paying side is willing to fund
The subsidy side is typically harder to acquire or more price-sensitive
Subsidy strategy must eventually lead to a sustainable revenue model

faq.question: How do platforms decide which side to subsidize?
faq.answer: Subsidize the side whose participation is more valuable to the other side, more price-sensitive, or harder to attract. Nightclubs let women in free because their presence attracts men who pay. Google subsidizes users because their searches attract advertiser spending.

faq.question: When should platform subsidies end?
faq.answer: Subsidies should decrease as network effects strengthen and the platform becomes self-sustaining. However, ending subsidies too early can stall growth, while maintaining them too long burns capital. The transition to profitability requires careful timing and alternative value creation.
